# Bulbar palsy and pseudobulbar palsy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Peripheral nerve disorders > Bulbar palsy and pseudobulbar palsy*

[Original Article Link](/library/nR07nf)

---

## Summary

<u>Bulbar palsy</u> is a <u>lower motor neuron</u> palsy that affects the <u>nuclei</u> of the IX<sup>th</sup>, X<sup>th</sup>, XI<sup>th</sup>, and XII<sup>th</sup> <u>cranial</u> nerves. <u>Pseudobulbar palsy</u> is an <u>upper motor neuron</u> palsy that affects the <u>corticobulbar tracts</u> of the V<sup>th</sup>, VII<sup>th</sup>, IX<sup>th</sup>, X<sup>th</sup>, XI<sup>th</sup>, and XII<sup>th</sup> <u>cranial</u> nerves. Any condition which disrupts or damages the <u>cranial nerve nuclei</u> or <u>corticobulbar tracts</u> can cause bulbar or <u>pseudobulbar palsy</u> (e.g., <u>stroke</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>, infections, <u>brain stem</u> tumors). Both bulbar and <u>pseudobulbar palsy</u> are seen mainly in men over 75 years old and present with <u>dysarthria</u> and <u>dysphagia</u>. In addition, patients with <u>pseudobulbar palsy</u> present with a lack of facial expression, difficulty chewing, and emotional lability. <u>Lower motor neuron signs</u> (<u>atrophy</u> and <u>fasciculations</u> of the <u>tongue</u>, absent <u>gag reflex</u>) differentiate <u>bulbar palsy</u> from <u>pseudobulbar palsy</u>, which presents with <u>upper motor neuron signs</u> (<u>spastic</u> <u>tongue</u>, exaggerated gag, and <u>jaw</u> jerk reflexes). Diagnosis is mainly clinical. <u>CSF analysis</u> and <u>MRI</u> of the <u>brain</u> help identify the etiology. Treatment is mainly supportive.

---

## Subtypes and variants

|  | Bulbar palsy | Pseudobulbar palsy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Etiology | <br><br>* <u>Brainstem</u> <u>stroke</u> or tumors<br><br>* <u>Neurodegenerative diseases</u>: <u>amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</u>, syringobulbia<br><br>* Autoimmune neuropathies: Guillain-Barré syndrome, <u>myasthenia gravis</u><br><br>* Infectious neuropathies: <u>poliomyelitis</u>, <u>diphtheria</u>, <u>neurosyphilis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Stroke</u> (multiple, recurrent <u>strokes</u>)<br><br>* <u>Neurodegenerative disease</u>: <u>amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</u>, <u>progressive supranuclear palsy</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u><br><br>* Injury or <u>malignancy</u> of the high <u>brainstem</u><br><br><br> |
| Pathophysiology | <br><br>* Bilateral damage or injury of the nerve <u>nuclei</u> of <u>cranial</u> nerves IX, X, XI, and XII<br><br>* <u>Lower motor neuron</u> palsy of the respective muscles<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Bilateral damage or injury of <u>corticobulbar tracts</u> to nerve <u>nuclei</u> of <u>cranial</u> nerves V, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII<br><br>* <u>Upper motor neuron</u> palsy of the respective muscles<br><br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br><br>* Facial expression: normal<br><br>* Speech: nasal<br><br>* <u>Dysphagia</u>, drooling, nasal <u>regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Tongue</u><br><br>* Wasting<br><br>* <u>Fasciculations</u><br><br>* Inability to protrude the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Palatal movement: absent<br><br>* <u>Gag reflex</u>: absent<br><br>* <u>Jaw</u> jerk: normal<br><br>* Emotions not affected<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Facial expressions: absent (expressionless face)<br><br>* Speech: <u>spastic</u> <u>dysarthria</u> (husky, nasal voice)<br><br>* Difficulty in chewing<br><br>* <u>Dysphagia</u>, drooling, and nasal <u>regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Tongue</u><br><br>* <u>Spastic</u>, pointed<br><br>* Difficulty in <u>tongue</u> protrusion due to <u>spasticity</u><br><br>* No wasting/<br><u>fasciculations</u><br><br>* Palatal movement: absent<br><br>* <u>Gag reflex</u>: brisk (exaggerated)<br><br>* <u>Jaw</u> jerk: exaggerated; clonic<br><br>* Pseudobulbar affect: emotional dysregulation with an affect that is out of <u>proportion</u>/incongruent with a situation (e.g., laughing hysterically after <u>hearing</u> devastating news)<br><br><br> |

## Diagnosis

<u>Bulbar palsy</u> and <u>pseudobulbar palsy</u> are <u>clinical diagnoses</u> based on clinical features. Tests are performed to diagnose the underlying condition.



* Investigations to diagnose the etiology

* <u>Serology</u> for <u>syphilis</u>, <u>poliomyelitis</u>

* <u>CSF analysis</u> for Guillain-Barré syndrome (<u>albuminocytologic dissociation</u>), <u>multiple sclerosis</u> (<u>oligoclonal bands</u>)

* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> for <u>stroke</u>, tumors, <u>syringobulbia</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>

---

## Treatment

* No known treatment for irreversible causes of bulbar/<u>pseudobulbar palsy</u>

* Supportive therapy

* <u>Anticholinergics</u> to control drooling

* <u>Baclofen</u> for <u>spasticity</u> of <u>pseudobulbar palsy</u>

* <u>Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy</u> tube (<u>PEG</u>): for patients with severe <u>dysphagia</u> or recurrent <u>aspiration pneumonia</u>

* <u>Speech and language therapy</u>

* <u>Tricyclic antidepressants</u>, <u>SSRIs</u>, or a combination of <u>dextromethorphan</u> hydrobromide and <u>quinidine</u> sulfate (Nuedexta): for patients with <u>pseudobulbar affect</u>

* Treat the underlying cause (see “Etiology” in table above)
